Crucifixion was an ancient method of judicial and military execution in which the victim was tied or nailed to a large wooden cross and left to hang until death from exhaustion, asphyxiation, or shock. Various ancient empires, including Carthage, Persia, and Egypt, practiced this method. The Romans formalized it as a punishment reserved for slaves, rebels, and non-citizens. It is most famous in history as the method by which Jesus was executed in Judaea under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate around thirty CE. The crucifixion of Jesus transformed the symbol from one of shame and degradation into the central icon of Christian faith and salvation theology. For two millennia, the cross has symbolized both Christ's sacrifice and redemption, making the crucifixion historically the most consequential execution in Western civilization.

Crucifixion was reserved for the lowest classes: slaves, brigands, rebels, and provincials. Roman citizens were executed by other methods. The condemned often carried the crossbar to the execution site, were beaten by soldiers, and were sometimes left for days as a public warning. Death could take hours to days, resulting from gradual asphyxiation, hemorrhage, shock, or organ failure. Legs were often broken to hasten death.

Jesus was executed at Golgotha, Aramaic for "the place of the skull," also called Calvary, just outside Jerusalem's walls. Before crucifixion, he was scourged, or whipped, by Roman soldiers and crowned with thorns in mockery of his claim to kingship. An inscription reading "INRI"—Latin for Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews—was placed above his head.

According to the Gospels, Jesus hung for six hours, uttering the Seven Last Words, including the Aramaic cry "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" The Gospels report miraculous accompaniments: three hours of darkness, an earthquake, and the tearing of the Temple's inner curtain from top to bottom. A Roman soldier confirmed death by piercing his side with a spear, producing blood and water. His body was removed by Joseph of Arimathea for burial.

Christian theology interprets crucifixion as vicarious atonement: Jesus's death as a sacrifice for humanity's sins, replacing the Temple's sacrificial system. The Resurrection, believed by Christians to have occurred three days later, transformed crucifixion from execution into redemptive event and foundation of Christian faith. The cross became the central Christian symbol, replacing shame with salvation and making the instrument of death the sign of victory.
